plain_rule_summary: A registered sale deed is an important ownership document, but disputes may still arise about vendor title, fraud, impersonation, consideration, boundaries, possession, or prior rights.
The seller generally cannot transfer better title than they actually have, so vendor title is an important fact.
Registration supports authenticity and legal formality, but does not automatically remove all factual disputes such as forgery, fraud, prior sale, or lack of authority.
Possession, payment, property description, boundaries, and mutation records may all become relevant.
common_missing_facts: Did the seller have clear title?
Is the property description or boundary disputed?
Was mutation completed after the sale?
Is there an allegation of fraud, impersonation, forged signature, or prior sale?
possible_rights: Possible right to rely on a valid registered sale deed.
Possible right to challenge a defective or fraudulent sale deed.
Possible right to seek protection of possession if lawfully held.
Possible right to seek correction of records or civil relief depending on facts.
possible_remedies: Verify the chain of title before and after the sale deed.
Collect registered sale deed, prior title documents, payment proof, and possession evidence.
If fraud or forgery is alleged, consult a lawyer immediately and preserve registration documents.
If possession is threatened, seek urgent local legal advice.
possible_outcomes: If the sale deed is valid and vendor title is established, the buyer's claim may become stronger.
If the seller lacked title or authority, the buyer's claim may face serious challenge.
If fraud, forgery, or impersonation is alleged, document authenticity becomes central.
If possession is disputed, interim protection or possession evidence may become important.
response_guidance: Do not say registration alone conclusively proves ownership.
Ask about vendor title, prior documents, possession, payment, and mutation.
Warn urgently if forgery, impersonation, or dispossession is alleged.
